logline: Tommy Norris works as a landman in West Texas - the fixer between roughnecks, wildcat billionaires, and cartel-adjacent criminals - navigating a Permian Basin oil boom that is simultaneously reshaping the economy and fuelling the violence around it.

bollymeter.basis: 78 percent Tomatometer with a 57 percent audience Popcornmeter - critics endorsed Thornton's lead performance while the audience split tracked ambivalence about whether Sheridan's West Texas oil framework added anything structurally new to his catalogue.

seasons.review_body: Landman launched November 17, 2024 on Paramount+, adapting Christian Wallace's podcast Boomtown into a 10-episode West Texas oil drama with Billy Bob Thornton as Tommy Norris - a landman who negotiates mineral rights while mediating between roughnecks, corporate interests, and cartel-adjacent criminal networks. Critics scored it at 78 percent on Rotten Tomatoes, with the consensus centred on Thornton's lived-in authority as the season's strongest argument. Reviewers were more divided on whether the Sheridan framework offered formal novelty beyond the Yellowstone template. The 57 percent audience Popcornmeter score tracked genuine viewer ambivalence about the show's tonal register and its commitment to the stoic-fixer-in-hostile-territory genre geometry.

episode_reviews.title: Landman
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series premiere establishes Tommy Norris in the Permian Basin field, immediately positioning him as the institutional fix-it figure between corporate oil interests and the criminal economy the boom sustains.

episode_reviews.title: Dreamers and Losers
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The second episode maps the full spectrum of West Texas oil ambition from wildcatter dreams to the quiet ruination of those the boom leaves behind.

episode_reviews.title: Hell Has a Front Yard
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The violence of the oil patch encroaches on domestic space as the episode makes clear that the Permian Basin's costs are not contained to the field.

episode_reviews.title: The Sting of Second Chances
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Tommy navigates the gap between the deal that salvages a situation and the one that merely defers its consequences - the landman's essential professional dilemma.

episode_reviews.title: Where Is Home
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode interrogates belonging for people whose work demands perpetual motion through territories that offer money but resist settlement.

episode_reviews.title: Beware the Second Beating
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: An escalating conflict from earlier in the season returns with compounded interest as the episode makes clear that the oil-patch economy of violence follows its own debt logic.

episode_reviews.title: All Roads Lead to a Hole
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season's narrative threads converge toward a reckoning as the episode's title collapses the distinction between a well drilled and a hole dug for other purposes.

episode_reviews.title: Clumsy, This Life
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The penultimate run of episodes confronts the domestic wreckage that the Norris family's oil-patch exposure has accumulated - a quieter hour in a series that earns its quieter moments.

episode_reviews.title: WolfCamp
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Named for the Wolfcamp shale formation that defines Permian Basin production, the episode ties the season's human drama to the geological logic underneath it.

episode_reviews.title: The Crumbs of Hope
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 1 finale distributes the aftermath of the season's confrontations with the unsentimental arithmetic the show has applied to hope throughout - some people get the crumbs, some get nothing.

bollymeter.basis: 83 percent Tomatometer reflects improved critical reception as the season's generational framing - Sam Elliott as Tommy's father, Andy Garcia as a cartel figure - gave the West Texas power dynamics a vertical dimension that Season 1 lacked.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 premiered November 16, 2025 with significant new additions: Sam Elliott as Tommy's father T.L. Norris and Andy Garcia as cartel figure Danny Morrell. Critics responded more warmly than Season 1, lifting the Tomatometer to 83 percent as the generational framing gave the show's West Texas power structure a new vertical dimension. Elliott's presence provided the show's masculine stoicism with a credible emotional genealogy, and Garcia's cartel thread deepened the criminal-versus-energy-company pressure that Season 1 had only gestured at. Several reviewers identified Season 2 as the point at which Landman distinguished itself from the broader Sheridan catalogue.
seasons.season_over_season: Adds generational depth via Sam Elliott and sharpens the cartel threat through Andy Garcia - critics lifted from 78 to 83 percent as the show found arguments Season 1 had only sketched.

episode_reviews.title: Death and a Sunset
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Season 2 opens with mortality and landscape framed together - a West Texas sunset over the consequences of the first season's final choices, with new family and new enemies waiting in the frame.

episode_reviews.title: Sins of the Father
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season's generational theme arrives in full as Tommy's relationship with T.L. Norris is established through the specific language of men who have hurt each other in ways neither names directly.

episode_reviews.title: Almost a Home
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode revisits the season's domestic question from a sharper angle: what constitutes home for people in a world that treats every place as a resource extraction site.

episode_reviews.title: Dancing Rainbows
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A title that holds irony against the Permian Basin's actual chromatics as the episode moves the cartel dimension of the season closer to the Norris family's daily orbit.

episode_reviews.title: The Pirate Dinner
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A meal becomes a negotiation and a negotiation becomes a threat display as the episode renders the social rituals of West Texas oil-patch power with the series' characteristic deadpan.

episode_reviews.title: Dark Night of the Soul
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season's moral reckoning deepens as the episode's St. John of the Cross reference frames Tommy's professional crisis in terms the show rarely uses: not strategic but spiritual.

episode_reviews.title: Forever Is an Instant
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A compressed time frame within the episode mirrors the season's broader argument about the oil-patch economy: fortunes and lives turn on decisions that take seconds and carry consequences that take years.

episode_reviews.title: Handsome Touched Me
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode's cryptic title opens onto a moment of unexpected physical grace inside a season that has delivered primarily violence - a tonal pivot the show earns with some difficulty.

episode_reviews.title: Plans, Tears and Sirens
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The penultimate episode assembles the season's three registers - strategic, emotional, operational - in a sequence that makes clear which of the three the finale will be asked to resolve.

episode_reviews.title: Tragedy and Flies
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 2 finale earns its title through the particular West Texas logic that tragedy and its attendant scavengers arrive together - not sequentially but simultaneously, and often in the same truck.
